question.text: If $D$ is the finite region enclosed by the curves $y=x^2$ and $y=-2x,$ as shown above, then $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} f(x,y)\, \mathrm{d}A =$
question.explanation:
First, let's represent $D$ as a type I region. To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

As a result, we get

\[ D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: -2 \leq x \leq 0, \quad x^2 \leq y \leq - 2x \big\}. \]

Therefore, we can express the integral, as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \, \mathrm{d}A &=\int_{-2}^{0} \int_{x^2}^{-2x} f(x,y) \, \mathrm{d}y \: \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\int_{-2}^{0} \left[ \int_{x^2}^{-2x} f(x,y) \, \mathrm{d}y \right] \mathrm{d}x \end{align*}

question.text: If $D$ is the finite region enclosed by the lines $y=2x,$ $y=6-x,$ and $x=0,$ then $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \, \mathrm{d}A =$
question.explanation:
First, let's make a sketch of our region.

Now, let's represent $D$ as a type I region.

  • To determine the $x$-limits, we need to find the $x$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $x\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} -x+6&=2x\\[5pt] %-3x &= -6\\[5pt] 3x &=6\\[5pt] x&=\dfrac{6}{3}\\[5pt] x&=2 \end{align*} So, $x$-limits are $ 0 \le x \le 2. $

  • To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

As a result, we get

\[ D = \left\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2, \quad 2x \leq y \leq 6-x \right\}. \]

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_D f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}A & = \int_0^2 \int_{2x}^{6-x} f(x,y) \ \mathrm{d}y \: \mathrm{d}x \end{align*}

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_D f\left( {x,y} \right)\,\mathrm{d}A &=\int_{-3}^1 \int_{x^2/2}^{3/2 - x} f(x,y) \ \mathrm{d}y \: \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\int_{-3}^1 \left[ \int_{x^2/2}^{3/2 - x} f(x,y) \ \mathrm{d}y \right] \mathrm{d}x \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Evaluating a Repeated Integral Defined Over a Type I Region

question.text: Calculate $\displaystyle \int_{0}^1\int_{x^2}^{2-x^2} {x}\,\mathrm dy\,\mathrm dx.$
question.explanation:
The integral is defined over a type I region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

\begin{align*} \displaystyle \int_{0}^1\int_{x^2}^{2-x^2} {x}\,\mathrm dy\,\mathrm dx &= \int_{0}^1 x\left[\int_{x^2}^{2-x^2} \mathrm dy \right]\,\mathrm dx \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^1 x \Big[ y \Big]_{x^2}^{2-x^2} \,\mathrm dx \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^1 x\left(2-x^2-x^2\right) \,\mathrm dx \\[5pt] &= 2\int_{0}^1 \left(x-x^3\right) \,\mathrm dx \end{align*}

Then, we integrate with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} 2\int_{0}^1 \left(x-x^3\right) \,\mathrm dx &= 2 \left[ \dfrac{x^2}{2} - \dfrac{x^4}{4}\right]_{0}^1 \\[5pt] &= 2 \left( \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{4} - 0 \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{align*}

question.text: Calculate $\displaystyle \int_{-1}^1\int_0^{|x|} (x+y^2) \,\mathrm dy\,\mathrm dx.$
question.explanation:
The integral is defined over a type I region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

\begin{align*} \int_{-1}^1\int_0^{|x|} (x+y^2) \,\mathrm dy\,\mathrm dx &= \int_{-1}^1\left[\int_0^{|x|} (x+y^2) \,\mathrm dy\right]\,\mathrm dx \\[5pt] &=\int_{-1}^1\left[ xy+\dfrac{y^3}{3}\right]_0^{|x|}\,\mathrm dx \\[5pt] &=\int_{-1}^1 \left( x\cdot|x|+\dfrac{|x|^3}{3} \right) \mathrm dx \end{align*}

Then, we integrate with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \int_{-1}^1 \left( x\cdot|x|+\dfrac{|x|^3}{3} \right) \mathrm dx &=\int_{-1}^0 \left( -x^2-\dfrac{x^3}{3} \right) \mathrm dx+ \int_0^1 \left( x^2+\dfrac{x^3}{3} \right) \mathrm dx \\[5pt] &=\left[-\dfrac{x^3}{3}- \dfrac{x^4}{12}\right]_{-1}^0+ \left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}+\dfrac{x^4}{12} \right]_0^1 \\[5pt] &=\left(0 -\dfrac{1}{3}+ \dfrac{1}{12}\right)+ \left(\dfrac{1}{3}+\dfrac{1}{12}-0\right) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{6} \end{align*}

example.title: Evaluating a Repeated Integral Defined Over a Type I Region

question.text: Calculate $\displaystyle \int_0^{1} \int_{-x^2-2}^{2-2x^2} 6x^3\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x.$
question.explanation:
The integral is defined over a type I region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

\begin{align*} \displaystyle \int_0^{1} \int_{-x^2-2}^{2-2x^2} 6x^3\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x &= \int_0^{1} 6x^3 \left[ \int_{-x^2-2}^{2-2x^2} \mathrm{d}y \right] \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{1} 6x^3 \left( 2-2x^2 - (-x^2-2) \right) \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] %&= \frac{1}{2}\int_0^{1} (x^{1/3+4} - x^{1/3+2})\,\mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{1} (-6x^5 + 24x^3)\,\mathrm{d}x \end{align*}

Then, we integrate with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \int_0^{1} (24x^3 - 6x^5)\,\mathrm{d}x &= \left[ 6x^4 - x^6 \right]_0^{1} \\[5pt] &= \left(6 - 1\right) - 0 \\[5pt] &= 5 \end{align*}

example.title: Evaluating a Repeated Integral Defined Over a Type I Region

question.text: Calculate $\displaystyle \int_{1/2}^{1} \int_{x}^{1/x} \dfrac{y}{x^2}\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x.$
question.explanation:
The integral is defined over a type I region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

\begin{align*} \displaystyle \int_{1/2}^{1} \int_{x}^{1/x} \dfrac{y}{x^2}\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x &= \int_{1/2}^{1} \dfrac{1}{x^2} \left[ \int_{x}^{1/x} y\,\mathrm{d}y \right] \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{1/2}^{1} \dfrac{1}{x^2} \left[ \dfrac{y^2}{2} \right]_{x}^{1/x} \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{1/2}^{1} \dfrac{1}{2x^2} \left(\dfrac{1}{x^2} - x^2 \right) \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \frac{1}{2}\int_{1/2}^{1} \left(\dfrac{1}{x^4} - 1 \right)\,\mathrm{d}x \end{align*}

Then, we integrate with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{1/2}^{1} \left(\dfrac{1}{x^4} - 1 \right)\,\mathrm{d}x &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[ -\dfrac{1}{3x^3} - x \right]_{1/2}^{1} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\left[ \dfrac{1}{3} + 1 - \left(\dfrac{8}{3} + \dfrac{1}{2} \right)\right] \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\left( -\dfrac{11}{6} \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{11}{12} \end{align*}

question.text: $\displaystyle \int_0^{2\pi}\int_{\sin x}^{1+\sin x} x^5 \,\mathrm dy\,\mathrm dx =$
question.explanation:
The integral is defined over a type I region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

\begin{align*} \int_0^{2\pi}\int_{\sin x}^{1+\sin x} x^5 \,\mathrm{d}y \: \mathrm{d}x &= \int_0^{2\pi} x^5 \left[ \int_{\sin x}^{1+\sin x} \,\mathrm{d}y \right] \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\int_0^{2\pi} x^5 \big[ y \big]_{\sin x}^{1+\sin x} \, \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\int_0^{2\pi} x^5 \big((1+\sin x) - \sin{x} \big) \,\mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\int_0^{2\pi}x^5 \,\mathrm{d}x \end{align*}

Then, we integrate with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \int_0^{2\pi} x^5 \,\mathrm{d}x &= \left[\dfrac{x^6}{6}\right]_0^{2\pi} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{(2\pi)^{6}}{6} - 0 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{32\pi^6}{3} \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating a Double Integral Defined Over a Type I Region

question.text: Evaluate the double integral $\displaystyle \iint \limits_{D} \mathrm{d}A,$ where $D$ is the finite region below the line $y=3$ enclosed by the lines $y=\dfrac{x}{3}$ and $x=6.$
question.explanation:
Notice that $D$ is a type I region.

  • We already know the intersection of the line $y=\dfrac{x}{3}$ with the line $y=3.$ So, the $x$-limits are $ 6 \le x \le 9. $

  • To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

As a result, the integral is defined over the following type I region:

\[ D = \Big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 6 \leq x \leq 9, \quad \dfrac{x}{3} \leq y \leq 3 \Big\} \]

So, we can express the integral, as follows:

\[ \iint \limits_{D} \mathrm{d}A = \int_6^9 \int_{x/3}^{3} \mathrm{d}y \: \mathrm{d}x \]

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

\begin{align*} \int_6^9 \int_{x/3}^{3} \mathrm{d}y \: \mathrm{d}x &= \int_6^9 \left[ \int_{x/3}^{3} \mathrm{d}y \right] \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_6^9 \Big[ y \Big]_{x/3}^{3} \,\mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_6^9 \left( 3- \dfrac{x}{3} \right) \,\mathrm{d}x \end{align*}

Then, we integrate with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \int_6^9 \left( 3 - \dfrac{x}{3} \right) \,\mathrm{d}x &= \left[ 3x - \dfrac{x^2}{6} \right]_6^9 \\[5pt] &=27 - \dfrac{81}{6} - \left(18 - \dfrac{36}{6}\right)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{2} \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating a Double Integral Defined Over a Type I Region

question.text: Calculate $\displaystyle \iint \limits_{D} x\, \mathrm{d}A,\:$ where $D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \: 2x^2 \leq y \leq x^2+1 \big\}.$
question.explanation:
The integral is defined over the type I region $D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \: 2x^2 \leq y \leq x^2+1 \big\}.$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint \limits_{D} x\, \mathrm{d}A &= \int_0^{1} \int_{2x^2}^{x^2+1} x \, \mathrm{d}y \: \mathrm{d}x \end{align*}

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

\begin{align*} \int_0^{1} \int_{2x^2}^{x^2+1} x \, \mathrm{d}y \: \mathrm{d}x &= \int_0^{1} x \left[ \int_{2x^2}^{x^2+1} \mathrm{d}y \right] \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} x \Big[ y \Big]_{2x^2}^{x^2+1} \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} x\left( x^2+1 - 2x^2 \right) \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} x\left( 1-x^2 \right) \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} \left( x - x^3 \right) \mathrm{d}x \end{align*}

Then, we integrate with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \int_{0}^{1} \left( x - x^3 \right) \mathrm{d}x &= \left[ \dfrac{x^2}{2} - \frac{x^4}{4} \right]_0^1 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{4} - 0 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{4} \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating a Double Integral Defined Over a Type I Region

question.text: Calculate $\displaystyle \iint \limits_{D} \dfrac{2y}{x}\, \mathrm{d}A,\:$ where $D = \left\{ (x,y) \: : \: \dfrac{1}{4} \leq x \leq \dfrac{1}{2}, \: x \leq y \leq 1-x \right\}.$
question.explanation:
The integral is defined over the type I region $D = \left\{ (x,y) \: : \: \dfrac{1}{4} \leq x \leq \dfrac{1}{2}, \: x \leq y \leq 1-x \right\}.$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint \limits_{D} \dfrac{2y}{x}\, \mathrm{d}A &= \int_{1/4}^{1/2} \int_{x}^{1-x} \dfrac{2y}{x} \, \mathrm{d}y \: \mathrm{d}x \end{align*}

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

\begin{align*} \int_{1/4}^{1/2} \int_{x}^{1-x} \dfrac{2y}{x} \, \mathrm{d}y \: \mathrm{d}x &= \int_{1/4}^{1/2} \dfrac{1}{x} \left[ \int_{x}^{1-x} 2y \, \mathrm{d}y \right] \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{1/4}^{1/2} \dfrac{1}{x} \Big[ y^2 \Big]_{x}^{1-x} \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{1/4}^{1/2} \dfrac{1}{x}\left( (1-x)^2 -x^2 \right) \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{1/4}^{1/2} \dfrac{1}{x}\left(1- 2x\right) \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{1/4}^{1/2} \left( \dfrac{1}{x}-2 \right) \mathrm{d}x \end{align*}

Then, we integrate with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \int_{1/4}^{1/2} \left( \dfrac{1}{x} -2\right) \mathrm{d}x &= \Big[ \ln{x}-2x \Big]_{1/4}^{1/2} \\[5pt] &= \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)-1 - \left(\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{2} +\ln{2} \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating a Double Integral Defined Over a Type I Region

question.text: Calculate $\displaystyle \iint \limits_{D}(1-y)\, \mathrm{d}A,\:$ where $D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \: x \leq y \leq \sqrt{x} \big\}.$
question.explanation:
The integral is defined over the type I region $D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \: x \leq y \leq \sqrt{x} \big\}.$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint \limits_{D} (1-y)\, \mathrm{d}A &= \int_0^{1} \int_{x}^{\sqrt{x}} (1-y) \, \mathrm{d}y \: \mathrm{d}x \end{align*}

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

\begin{align*} \int_0^{1} \int_{x}^{\sqrt{x}} (1-y) \, \mathrm{d}y \: \mathrm{d}x &= \int_0^{1} \left[ \int_{x}^{\sqrt{x}} (1-y) \, \mathrm{d}y \right] \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} \left[ y - \dfrac{1}{2}y^2 \right]_{x}^{\sqrt{x}} \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} \left( \sqrt{x} - \dfrac{1}{2}(\sqrt{x})^2 - x + \dfrac{1}{2}x^2 \right) \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} \left( \sqrt{x} - \dfrac{3}{2}x + \dfrac{1}{2}x^2 \right) \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1} \left(2\sqrt{x} - 3x + x^2\right) \mathrm{d}x \end{align*}

Then, we integrate with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{1} \left( 2\sqrt{x} - 3x + x^2\right) \mathrm{d}x & = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{1} \left( 2x^{1/2} - 3x + x^2\right) \mathrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[ \dfrac{4}{3}x^{3/2} - \dfrac{3}{2}x^2 +\dfrac{1}{3}x^3 \right]_0^1\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left( \dfrac{4}{3}(1)^{3/2}- \dfrac{3}{2}(1)^2 + \dfrac{1}{3}(1)^3 \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{4}{3} - \dfrac{3}{2} + \dfrac{1}{3} \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{6} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{12} \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating a Double Integral Defined Over a Type I Region

question.text: Calculate $\displaystyle \iint \limits_{D} \frac{e^{2y}}{x}\, \mathrm{d}A,$ where $D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 1 \leq x \leq 5, \: \ln x \leq y \leq 3 \big\}.$
question.explanation:
The integral is defined over the type I region $D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 1 \leq x \leq 5, \: \ln x \leq y \leq 3 \big\}.$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint \limits_{D} \frac{e^{2y}}{x}\, \mathrm{d}A &= \int_1^{5} \int_{\ln x}^{3} \dfrac{e^{2y}}{x} \, \mathrm{d}y \: \mathrm{d}x \end{align*}

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

\begin{align*} \int_1^{5} \int_{\ln x}^{3} \frac{e^{2y}}{x} \, \mathrm{d}y \: \mathrm{d}x &= \int_1^{5} \dfrac{1}{x} \left[ \int_{\ln x}^{3} e^{2y} \, \mathrm{d}y \right] \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{1}^{5} \dfrac{1}{x} \left[ \frac{1}{2} e^{2y} \right]_{\ln x}^{3} \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \frac{1}{2 }\int_{1}^{5} \left( \frac{e^6}{x} - \frac{e^{2\ln x}}{x} \right) \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \frac{1}{2}\int_{1}^{5} \left( \frac{e^6}{x} - \frac{x^2}{x} \right) \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \frac{1}{2}\int_{1}^{5} \left( \frac{e^6}{x} - x \right) \mathrm{d}x \end{align*}

Then, we integrate with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \frac{1}{2}\int_{1}^{5} \left( \frac{e^6}{x} - x \right) \mathrm{d}x &= \frac{1}{2} \left[ e^6 \ln x - \frac{x^2}{2} \right]_1^5 \\[5pt] &=\frac{1}{2} \left( \left( e^6 \ln(5) - \frac{25}{2} \right) - \left( e^6 \ln(1) - \frac{1}{2} \right) \right) \\[5pt] &= \frac{e^6 \ln 5}{2} - 6 \end{align*}
